messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Seventy-six-year-old Giovanni had always taken pride in his work as a hotel manager. He knew every inch of the building, every staff member by name, and every guest's preference. But it all changed one fateful day when a toxic chemical leak occurred in the hotel's basement, exposing him to noxious fumes. As he struggled to evacuate guests and employees, Giovanni couldn't shake off the feeling that his body had betrayed him. The once-familiar surroundings now seemed treacherous, and his own physical reactions, unpredictable. In the months following the incident, Giovanni found himself increasingly on edge, even in the safety of his own home. He would constantly monitor his thoughts for signs of "going crazy," a fear fueled by his conviction that his body was no longer reliable. His senses were perpetually heightened, and unexpected sounds – the creaking of floorboards or the hum of the refrigerator – made him jump. Giovanni's world had shrunk to a handful of "safe zones" where he felt some semblance of control. The rest of the world seemed like a minefield. Giovanni's memories of that day were fragmented and disjointed, like pieces of a puzzle that refused to fit together. He would recall the acrid smell of chemicals, only to have it vanish without warning. Other times, he'd feel an overwhelming sense of dread without any clear image or memory attached. These disjointed recollections kept him up at night, his mind racing with worst-case scenarios. As Giovanni struggled to make sense of these fragmented memories, he began to avoid the hotel altogether. The mere thought of stepping foot in that building sent his anxiety soaring. He'd try to distract himself with loud music or TV, but the sounds only seemed to amplify his unease. Giovanni felt trapped in a cycle of fear and avoidance, unable to escape the grip of his own memories. His negative appraisals of himself and his body – "My body keeps reacting as if I'm still in danger even when I'm safe" – reinforced this sense of helplessness. Giovanni couldn't shake off the feeling that he was at the mercy of his own reactions, powerless to stop bad things from happening to him. As the days turned into weeks, and the weeks into months, Giovanni's world continued to shrink. His relationships suffered, and even simple tasks seemed insurmountable. It wasn't until a particularly harrowing episode – where he found himself crippled by anxiety in the middle of his own living room – that Giovanni realized he needed help. He couldn't continue living like this, trapped in a never-ending cycle of fear and avoidance. What finally brought Giovanni to seek therapy was the realization that he was losing himself in this labyrinth of memories and fears. He longed for a sense of control over his body and mind, to be able to trust himself again. As he sat in the therapist's office, fidgeting with his hands, Giovanni whispered, "I just want to feel safe in my own skin."
